source.text: Ἄγουσιν οὖν τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἀπὸ τοῦ Καϊάφα εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον· ἦν δὲ πρωΐ· καὶ αὐτοὶ οὐκ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον, ἵνα μὴ μιανθῶσιν ἀλλὰ φάγωσιν τὸ πάσχα.

records.literal_gloss: They lead therefore the Jesus from the Caiaphas into the praetorium; it was now early; and they not entered into the praetorium, that not they might be defiled but might eat the Passover.

en.L: So they lead Jesus from Caiaphas into the praetorium. Now it was early. And they themselves did not enter into the praetorium, so that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.
en.B: Then they led Jesus from Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They did not go into the headquarters themselves, to avoid becoming ritually unclean, since they wanted to eat the Passover.
en.R: Then they took Jesus from Caiaphas to the palace of the Roman governor. It was very early in the morning. The men who had brought {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} did not go inside the palace. They wanted to stay ritually clean so that they could eat the Passover meal.

es.L: Conducen, pues, a Jesús desde Caifás al pretorio; y era temprano. Y ellos mismos no entraron en el pretorio, para no quedar impuros, sino poder comer la Pascua.
es.B: Luego llevaron a Jesús de la casa de Caifás a la residencia del gobernador. Era muy de mañana. Ellos mismos no entraron en la residencia, para no quedar ritualmente impuros, porque querían comer la Pascua.
es.R: Después llevaron a Jesús de la casa de Caifás al palacio del gobernador romano. Era muy temprano por la mañana. Los que habían llevado a Jesús no entraron en el palacio. Querían seguir ritualmente puros para poder comer la cena de la Pascua.

fr.L: Ils mènent donc Jésus de chez Caïphe au prétoire. Or il était tôt. Et eux-mêmes n’entrèrent pas dans le prétoire, afin de ne pas être souillés, mais de manger la Pâque.
fr.B: Puis ils conduisirent Jésus de chez Caïphe au palais du gouverneur. C’était au petit matin. Eux-mêmes n’entrèrent pas dans le palais, pour ne pas devenir rituellement impurs, car ils voulaient manger la Pâque.
fr.R: Ensuite, ils ont emmené Jésus de chez Caïphe au palais du gouverneur romain. C’était très tôt le matin. Les hommes qui {{deity_pronoun:l’|L’}}avaient amené ne sont pas entrés dans le palais. Ils voulaient rester purs selon les règles religieuses, pour pouvoir manger le repas de la Pâque.

sw.L: Basi wanampeleka Yesu kutoka kwa Kayafa hadi ikulu. Na ilikuwa mapema. Na wao wenyewe hawakuingia ikulu, ili wasitiwe unajisi, bali waweze kula Pasaka.
sw.B: Kisha walimpeleka Yesu kutoka kwa Kayafa hadi ikulu ya mkuu wa mkoa. Ilikuwa asubuhi na mapema. Wao wenyewe hawakuingia ikulu, ili wasiwe najisi kidini, kwa sababu walitaka kula Pasaka.
sw.R: Kisha walimchukua Yesu kutoka kwa Kayafa, wakampeleka kwenye ikulu ya mkuu wa mkoa wa Kirumi. Ilikuwa asubuhi mapema sana. Wale watu waliomleta hawakuingia ndani ya ikulu. Walitaka kubaki safi kwa desturi ya dini ili waweze kula chakula cha Pasaka.

vi.L: Vậy họ dẫn Đức Giê-xu từ chỗ Cai-phe đến dinh tổng đốc. Lúc ấy trời còn sớm. Còn chính họ thì không vào dinh tổng đốc, để khỏi bị ô uế, nhưng [còn] được ăn Lễ Vượt Qua.
vi.B: Sau đó, họ giải Đức Giê-xu từ nhà Cai-phe đến dinh tổng đốc. Khi ấy trời vừa rạng sáng. Chính họ không vào trong dinh, để khỏi bị ô uế theo nghi lễ, vì họ muốn ăn bữa Lễ Vượt Qua.
vi.R: Rồi họ đưa Đức Giê-xu từ nhà Cai-phe đến dinh của quan tổng đốc La Mã. Lúc đó trời còn rất sớm. Những người giải {{deity_pronoun:ngài|Ngài}} đến không vào trong dinh. Họ muốn giữ mình tinh sạch theo nghi lễ để có thể ăn bữa Lễ Vượt Qua.

ko.L: 그래서 그들이 예수를 가야바에게서 관정으로 끌고 간다. 때는 이른 새벽이었다. 그리고 그들 자신은 관정 안으로 들어가지 않았다. 더럽혀지지 않고 유월절 [음식]을 먹으려는 것이었다.
ko.B: 그들은 예수를 가야바에게서 총독 관저로 끌고 갔다. 이른 아침이었다. 그들은 정결 규정에 따라 부정해지지 않으려고 관저 안으로는 들어가지 않았다. 유월절 음식을 먹어야 했기 때문이다.
ko.R: 그 사람들은 예수를 가야바의 집에서 로마 총독이 머무는 관저로 데려갔다. 아주 이른 아침이었다. 예수를 끌고 온 사람들은 관저 안으로 들어가지 않았다. 율법에 따라 몸을 깨끗하게 지켜야 유월절 음식을 먹을 수 있었기 때문이다.

pt.L: Levam, então, Jesus da casa de Caifás para o pretório. E era de madrugada. E eles mesmos não entraram no pretório, para não se contaminarem, mas poderem comer a Páscoa.
pt.B: Então levaram Jesus da casa de Caifás para o quartel do governador. Era bem cedo. Eles mesmos não entraram no quartel, para não ficarem ritualmente impuros, pois queriam comer a Páscoa.
pt.R: Depois levaram Jesus da casa de Caifás para o palácio do governador romano. Era muito cedo, de manhãzinha. Os homens que tinham levado Jesus não entraram no palácio. Eles queriam continuar ritualmente puros para poderem comer a ceia da Páscoa.

am.L: ስለዚህ ኢየሱስን ከቀያፋ ዘንድ ወደ ፕራይቶሪዮን ይወስዱታል፤ ማለዳም ነበር፤ እነርሱም እንዳይረክሱ ነገር ግን ፋሲካን እንዲበሉ ወደ ፕራይቶሪዮን አልገቡም።
am.B: ከዚያም ኢየሱስን ከቀያፋ ዘንድ ወደ አገረ ገዡ መኖሪያ ግቢ ወሰዱት። ጊዜው ማለዳ ነበር። እነርሱ ግን በሥርዓቱ እንዳይረክሱ ወደ መኖሪያ ግቢው አልገቡም፤ ፋሲካን መብላት ይፈልጉ ነበርና።
am.R: ከዚያም ኢየሱስን ከቀያፋ ዘንድ ወደ ሮማዊው አገረ ገዥ ቤተ መንግሥት ወሰዱት። ገና በጣም ማለዳ ነበር። ኢየሱስን ያመጡት ሰዎች ወደ ቤተ መንግሥቱ ውስጥ አልገቡም። የፋሲካን ራት መብላት እንዲችሉ በሥርዓቱ ንጹሕ ሆነው መቆየት ፈልገው ነበር።

decisions.choice: the praetorium: the headquarters of the Roman governor
decisions.reason: The word is a Latin military term taken into Greek. It was first a general's tent, then the residence and headquarters of a Roman governor (Matthew 27:27; Acts 23:35). The governor of Judea normally lived at Caesarea on the coast and came up to Jerusalem at the great festivals. Whether his Jerusalem headquarters was the former palace of Herod the Great or the Antonia fortress beside the temple is not known for certain.

decisions.choice: early: the last part of the night, around dawn
decisions.reason: The word names the last of the four watches of the night, after the rooster crows (Mark 13:35); the rooster had just crowed (18:27). Jesus is brought to the governor at first light.

decisions.choice: defiled: made ritually unclean by entering a Gentile's dwelling
decisions.reason: The defilement is ritual, not moral. Jews held that going into the house of a Gentile made a person unclean (Acts 10:28; 11:3); later Jewish teaching, collected in the Mishnah, counts the dwellings of Gentiles as unclean (Oholot 18:7). A person who was unclean could not eat the Passover at its proper time (Numbers 9:6-13). John sets their care over ritual purity beside their pressing for an innocent man's death.

decisions.choice: eat the Passover: the Passover meal, still ahead on the day of the trial
alternatives: the festival offerings eaten during the following days of the feast
decisions.reason: In John the Passover meal has not yet been eaten when Jesus is tried and crucified: the day is "the day of Preparation of the Passover" (19:14), and the Sabbath that follows is "a great day" (19:31). In Matthew, Mark and Luke, the meal Jesus ate with his disciples the night before was a Passover meal (Mark 14:12-16; Luke 22:15). The phrase can also mean the festival meals eaten during the seven days of the feast (compare 2 Chronicles 30:21-22), and on that reading the accounts agree in their timing. How they fit together is not settled here; the plain sense of John is followed.

decisions.choice: they: those who held Jesus at Caiaphas's house, the chief priests and their officers
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject; it carries on from 18:24-27. Pilate later says that the chief priests handed Jesus over (18:35), and the chief priests and their officers are the ones who shout for his crucifixion (19:6). "They themselves" sets these men, who stay outside, against Jesus, who is taken in.

decisions.choice: Historic present: they lead, says (L); led, said (B, R)
decisions.reason: John often tells past events in the present tense to make them vivid ("they lead", "he says"). Literal keeps the present throughout this passage so that readers see the Greek form; Balanced and Readable use the past, the normal tense for telling a story in English. This decision covers every historic present in 18:28-40 (also "says" in 18:29 and 18:38).

decisions.choice: the governor's headquarters (B); the palace of the Roman governor (R)
decisions.reason: "Praetorium" is a Latin word few readers know, so Balanced and Readable say what the building was (meaning decision m1). Readable names the governor as Roman, since the story turns on the difference between the Jewish authorities and the Roman court. Verse 33 uses the same words.

decisions.choice: to avoid becoming ritually unclean (B); the men who had brought him, stay ritually clean, the Passover meal (R)
alternatives: so that they would not be defiled
decisions.reason: "Defiled" could be taken as moral corruption, so Balanced and Readable say it was a matter of ritual cleanness (meaning decision m3). Readable names the subject as the men who had brought Jesus, without saying more than the text (meaning decision m5), and says "meal" for the Passover (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: historic present at Literal (conducen, dice); pretérito at Balanced and Readable
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in John: Literal keeps John's present, which makes the scene vivid; Balanced and Readable use the pretérito, as Spanish stories are told. This applies throughout the passage.

decisions.choice: el pretorio (L); la residencia del gobernador (B); el palacio del gobernador romano (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Latin word; Balanced and Readable say what the building was (meaning decision m1), and Readable names the governor as Roman, as in English. Literal "desde Caifás" keeps the Greek, which names the man, not his house.

decisions.choice: quedar impuros (L); ritualmente impuros (B); Los que habían llevado a Jesús, ritualmente puros, la cena de la Pascua (R)
decisions.reason: "Contaminarse" can sound like physical or moral corruption; the defilement is ritual (meaning decision m3), which Balanced and Readable say. As in English, Readable names the subject (meaning decision m5) and says that the Passover here is the meal (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: narration in the passé simple (L, B), with Literal keeping John's present tense ("ils mènent", "il dit"); passé composé (R); speech in the passé composé at every level
decisions.reason: The French brief for the passage (18:28-40). The passé simple ("conduisirent", "répondit") is the normal tense of written narrative and suits a public reading; Literal uses it for the Greek past tenses and keeps the present where John tells a past event in the present (18:28 "ils mènent", 18:29 and 18:38 "il dit"), as the English Literal does. Readable uses the passé composé ("ils ont emmené"), the past tense French readers speak and learn first. Inside speech every level uses the passé composé ("qu'as-tu fait ?").

decisions.choice: le prétoire (L); le palais du gouverneur (B); le palais du gouverneur romain (R)
decisions.reason: "Prétoire" is the French form of the Latin word and is known from church usage, but few readers know what it was; Balanced and Readable name the building (meaning decision m1). "Palais" fits the governor's residence in Jerusalem, whichever building it was; "quartier général" sounds modern and military. The same words are used in 18:33 and 19:9.

decisions.choice: L keeps the historic present where the Greek has it ("wanampeleka", "anasema" 18:29, "anamwambia" 18:38); B tells the story with -li- for the first verb and -ka- for those that follow; R uses the plain past
decisions.reason: As the English (rendering decision r-en-1): Literal keeps John's vivid present; Balanced and Readable use the narrative past, which is how written Swahili tells a story. This holds for the whole passage. As elsewhere, deity_pronoun spans go only on free pronouns and possessives ("wewe", "mimi", "wangu", "yake"), since a verb prefix cannot take a capital.

decisions.choice: ikulu (L); ikulu ya mkuu wa mkoa (B); ikulu ya mkuu wa mkoa wa Kirumi (R)
decisions.reason: "Ikulu" is the official residence of a ruler, which is what the praetorium was (meaning decision m1); Balanced and Readable say whose it was, as the English does. The same words are used through John 18-19.

decisions.choice: wasitiwe unajisi (L); wasiwe najisi kidini (B); kubaki safi kwa desturi ya dini (R)
decisions.reason: The defilement is ritual, not moral (meaning decision m3). "Unajisi" is the Swahili word for ritual uncleanness; Balanced adds "kidini" and Readable says it plainly, as the English does.

decisions.choice: "họ dẫn" with no past marker (L); "họ giải", "họ đưa" told as past by the time words "Sau đó", "Rồi" (B, R)
decisions.reason: Vietnamese verbs do not change for tense. Literal keeps John's historic present simply by leaving out "đã" here and throughout this passage ("Phi-lát nói", "Phi-lát hỏi"); Balanced and Readable let time words carry the past.

decisions.choice: "dinh tổng đốc" (L, B); "dinh của quan tổng đốc La Mã" (R)
decisions.reason: A Latin loanword would mean nothing to most readers; "dinh tổng đốc" (the governor's residence and seat) says what the praetorium was. Readable adds that the governor was Roman. Used the same way through John 18-19.

decisions.choice: historic present "끌고 간다", "말한다" (L); past (B, R), through this passage
decisions.reason: Literal keeps John's present tense in narrative (18:28, 29, 38; 19:4-15 has more), which Korean can use for vividness; Balanced and Readable tell the story in the past. One decision for 18:28-40.

decisions.choice: "관정" (L); "총독 관저" (B); "로마 총독이 머무는 관저" (R)
decisions.reason: A transliteration of the Latin word would mean nothing to Korean readers. Literal keeps the short traditional term for the governor's court; Balanced and Readable say what the building was. Used the same way through John 18-19.

decisions.choice: No deity_pronoun spans in Korean; the narrator uses "예수께서" and the honorific -시- for Jesus
alternatives: capitalised pronoun spans as in English
decisions.reason: Korean has no capital letters, so the setting has nothing to change (style guide, section 7). Recorded once for this passage.

decisions.choice: da casa de Caifás
decisions.reason: Portuguese "levar alguém de Caifás" does not say from where; "da casa de Caifás" gives the plain sense of the Greek "from Caiaphas" (meaning decision m5), and Literal needs no bracket because the preposition alone would not be read as a place.

decisions.choice: o pretório (L); o quartel do governador (B); o palácio do governador romano (R)
decisions.reason: As in Matthew 27:27: Literal keeps the Latin word, which Portuguese has; Balanced and Readable say what the building was (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: No deity_pronoun spans in the Amharic
alternatives: Marking pronouns for God and Jesus in some other way
decisions.reason: The Ethiopic script has no capital letters, so the setting that capitalises pronouns for God and Jesus in English has nothing to change in Amharic; most such pronouns are verb suffixes in any case.

decisions.choice: "ፕራይቶሪዮን" (L), "የአገረ ገዡ መኖሪያ ግቢ" (the governor's residence, B), "የአገረ ገዥ ቤተ መንግሥት" (the governor's palace, R); also 18:33 and 19:9
decisions.reason: As in Matthew 27:27: Literal keeps the Latin name of the governor's residence, as the English Literal does; Balanced and Readable say what it was.

source.text: ἐξῆλθεν οὖν ὁ Πιλᾶτος ἔξω πρὸς αὐτοὺς καὶ φησίν· Τίνα κατηγορίαν φέρετε κατὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τούτου;

records.literal_gloss: Went out therefore the Pilate outside to them and says, "What accusation do you bring against the man this?"

en.L: So Pilate went out to them and says, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
en.B: So Pilate came outside to them and asked, "What charge are you making against this man?"
en.R: So Pilate came out to meet them. "What do you accuse this man of?" he asked.

es.L: Salió, pues, Pilato afuera hacia ellos, y dice: «¿Qué acusación {{plural_you:traen|traéis}} contra este hombre?».
es.B: Así que Pilato salió adonde estaban ellos y les preguntó: «¿Qué cargo {{plural_you:presentan|presentáis}} contra este hombre?».
es.R: Entonces Pilato salió a hablar con ellos. «¿De qué {{plural_you:acusan|acusáis}} a este hombre?», les preguntó.

fr.L: Pilate sortit donc dehors vers eux, et il dit : « Quelle accusation portez-vous contre cet homme ? »
fr.B: Pilate sortit donc vers eux et demanda : « Quelle accusation portez-vous contre cet homme ? »
fr.R: Alors Pilate est sorti pour leur parler. « De quoi accusez-vous cet homme ? » a-t-il demandé.

sw.L: Basi Pilato alitoka nje kwao, na anasema, "Mnaleta mashtaka gani dhidi ya mtu huyu?"
sw.B: Basi Pilato alitoka nje kwao, akauliza, "Mnamshtaki mtu huyu kwa kosa gani?"
sw.R: Basi Pilato alitoka nje kukutana nao. Akauliza, "Mtu huyu mnamshtaki kwa kosa gani?"

vi.L: Vậy Phi-lát đi ra ngoài gặp họ và nói: "Các ông đem lời buộc tội gì chống lại người này?"
vi.B: Vì thế Phi-lát ra ngoài gặp họ và hỏi: "Các ông buộc tội người này về điều gì?"
vi.R: Phi-lát bèn ra ngoài gặp họ. Ông hỏi: "Người này đã làm gì mà các ông tố cáo?"

ko.L: 그래서 빌라도가 밖으로 그들에게 나가서 말한다. "너희는 이 사람에 대하여 무슨 고발을 하느냐?"
ko.B: 그래서 빌라도가 그들에게로 밖에 나와서 물었다. "너희는 이 사람을 무슨 죄로 고발하느냐?"
ko.R: 그래서 빌라도가 그들을 만나러 밖으로 나왔다. 그리고 물었다. "이 사람이 무슨 잘못을 했다고 고발하는 것이냐?"

pt.L: Pilatos, então, saiu até eles e diz: "Que acusação vocês trazem contra este homem?"
pt.B: Então Pilatos saiu ao encontro deles e perguntou: "De que vocês acusam este homem?"
pt.R: Então Pilatos saiu para falar com eles. "De que vocês acusam este homem?", perguntou ele.

am.L: ስለዚህ ጲላጦስ ወደ እነርሱ ወደ ውጭ ወጥቶ፦ «በዚህ ሰው ላይ የምታቀርቡት ክስ ምንድን ነው?» ይላል።
am.B: ስለዚህ ጲላጦስ ወደ እነርሱ ወደ ውጭ ወጥቶ፦ «በዚህ ሰው ላይ የምታቀርቡት ክስ ምንድን ነው?» ብሎ ጠየቀ።
am.R: ስለዚህ ጲላጦስ ሊያገኛቸው ወደ ውጭ ወጣ። «ይህን ሰው በምን ትከሱታላችሁ?» ብሎ ጠየቀ።

decisions.choice: Pilate: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea
decisions.reason: Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36 (Luke 3:1). A stone inscription found at Caesarea in 1961 calls him "prefect of Judea". John brings him into the story without introduction, as a figure his readers knew. Only the governor could order an execution (18:31).

decisions.choice: went out ... outside: the scene moves between the courtyard outside and the headquarters inside
decisions.reason: Because the accusers will not come in (18:28), Pilate goes back and forth: out to them here, in to Jesus (18:33), out again (18:38), in (19:9), out (19:4, 13). The doubled "went out outside" marks the first move. The questioning of Jesus happens inside; the shouting happens outside.

decisions.choice: accusation: a formal charge brought before a judge
decisions.reason: The word is a legal one. Pilate opens a hearing in proper form by asking for the charge.

decisions.choice: What charge are you making (B); What do you accuse this man of (R)
decisions.reason: Plain modern words for the legal question (meaning decision m3). The historic present "says" is covered by decision r-en-1 at 18:28.

decisions.choice: salió afuera (L); acusación (L), cargo (B), De qué acusan (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the doubled "went out outside" (meaning decision m2). Pilate asks in legal form for the charge (meaning decision m3); each level uses a word of the court.

decisions.choice: sortit dehors (L); sortit (B, R)
decisions.reason: French usually counts "sortir dehors" as a redundancy, but it shows the doubled Greek wording that marks Pilate's first move out of the building (meaning decision m2), so Literal keeps it. Balanced and Readable say it once.

decisions.choice: Pilate to the accusers: "tôi" for himself, "các ông" for them; Jesus is "người này" or "ông ta" in their talk
decisions.reason: Vietnamese must choose pronouns that show the relation. A Roman governor speaking to the Jewish leaders is formal but not insulting: "tôi" / "các ông". "ta" / "các ngươi" is the old mandarin register and sounds archaic. Kept through John 18:28-19:16.

decisions.choice: Pilate speaks to the accusers in the plain style (해라체: "고발하느냐")
decisions.reason: Pilate is the Roman governor and the judge; the style guide's default to those below one is 해라체. The same through John 18-19.

decisions.choice: Pilate addresses the Jewish leaders with the plain plural "እናንተ" (ትከሱታላችሁ)
decisions.reason: Pilate is the ruler and they are his subjects, so he speaks to them plainly, as in Matthew 27:17; they answer him with the respectful "እርስዎ" (18:30).

decisions.choice: were not doing evil: a man who habitually does wrong, a wrongdoer
decisions.reason: The verb "to be" with the participle "doing" describes an ongoing practice. They name no crime. Pilate asked for a charge (18:29); they answer that their own handing over should be proof enough.

decisions.choice: handed over: the word used again and again for Jesus's betrayal and surrender
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of Judas (18:2, 5), of the chief priests (18:35), of what Jesus' servants would have prevented (18:36), and of Pilate himself (19:16). It traces the chain by which Jesus is passed from hand to hand to the cross.

decisions.choice: handed over, at every level
decisions.reason: One English phrase is kept for this verb through the passion story so that readers can follow the chain (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: We would not have handed him over to you if this man were not a wrongdoer (B); He is a criminal ... If he were not (R)
alternatives: If this man were not doing evil (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the main clause first and uses a noun for the ongoing practice (meaning decision m1). Readable states the claim first in a short sentence; it says no more than "doing evil" implies.

decisions.choice: entregado, at every level; estuviera haciendo el mal (L), malhechor (B), criminal (R)
decisions.reason: "Entregar" is kept at every level for this verb through the passion story, so that readers can follow Jesus passed from hand to hand (meaning decision m2). Balanced and Readable use a noun for the ongoing practice (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: livrer, at every level
decisions.reason: One French verb is kept for this Greek verb through the passion story (18:30, 35, 36; 19:11, 16), so that readers can follow the chain by which Jesus is passed from hand to hand (meaning decision m2). "Livrer" is also the word used for Judas's betrayal; "remettre" would be lighter and lose the link.

decisions.choice: s'il ne faisait pas le mal (imperfect)
alternatives: s'il n'était pas en train de faire le mal
s'il n'était pas un homme faisant le mal
decisions.reason: The French imperfect already says an ongoing practice (meaning decision m1), so Literal needs no heavier phrase.

decisions.choice: kukabidhi at every level for the handing over of Jesus by the authorities and by Pilate (18:30, 35, 36; 19:11, 16)
alternatives: kumtoa, the Literal word for Judas's handing over (18:2, 5; 6:64)
decisions.reason: One verb is kept for this chain through the passion story (meaning decision m2), as the English keeps "handed over". "Kukabidhi" is the plain word for handing a person over to an authority. Judas's act keeps "kumtoa" at Literal and "kumsaliti" at Balanced and Readable, as earlier in John, so Swahili Literal shows the link less clearly than the English; a reviewer may prefer one verb for both.

decisions.choice: "quan" for "you" (Pilate), "chúng tôi" for the speakers
decisions.reason: Subjects address an official as "quan". "ngài" would also be respectful, but in this book "ngài" is the deity pronoun, so it is kept for Jesus and God.

decisions.choice: "ông ta" with no deity_pronoun span
decisions.reason: The English marks "him" for the capitalisation setting. In Vietnamese the speakers' own word for Jesus is "ông ta" or "người này", which shows their view of him and is not a deity pronoun, so there is nothing to capitalise. The same holds wherever opponents or Pilate speak of or to Jesus in this passage.

decisions.choice: the accusers speak to Pilate in 합쇼체 and say "총독님" for "you" ([총독님] at L)
decisions.reason: Korean does not address a superior as "you"; "당신" would be rude to a governor. "총독님" is the plain respectful title, bracketed in Literal because the Greek has only the pronoun.

decisions.choice: "넘겨주다" for paradidomi at every level, here and through the trial
decisions.reason: The same verb is used for Judas's betrayal and for each hand-over of Jesus (18:35, 36; 19:11, 16); one Korean verb lets the reader follow it.

decisions.choice: o senhor (the Jewish leaders to Pilate)
decisions.reason: The leaders speak up to the Roman governor, so they say "o senhor", as Brazilians address an authority (style section 4); "você" would sound insolent, and "tu" is kept for God and Jesus. Pilate says "vocês" to them and "tu" to Jesus; Jesus says "você" to Pilate, as in Matthew 27:11.

decisions.choice: entregar, at every level, through the passion story
decisions.reason: One Portuguese verb for this Greek verb, as the English keeps "hand over", so that readers can follow the chain from Judas to Pilate (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: The Jewish leaders address Pilate with the respectful "እርስዎ" (ለእርስዎ); also 18:40, 19:6, 19:12 and 19:15
decisions.reason: Subjects speaking to a ruler say "እርስዎ" in Amharic, as the slaves and subjects do in Matthew 27:63; Pilate and Jesus speak to each other with "አንተ".

decisions.choice: you take him: the stressed "you" pushes the case back to them
decisions.reason: "You" is added in Greek where it is not needed, which stresses it. Since they have named no crime against Roman law, Pilate tells them to deal with the man themselves.

decisions.choice: your law: the Law of Moses, applied in the Jewish courts
decisions.reason: Rome let the peoples it ruled settle many matters by their own laws and courts. In Judea the high priest and the council judged cases under the Law of Moses. Pilate treats the matter as an internal religious dispute.

decisions.choice: judge: try in court and give a verdict
decisions.reason: The verb has its legal sense here, as in 7:51 ("Does our law judge a man without first hearing him?").

decisions.choice: try (B); put on trial (R)
decisions.reason: In modern English "judge" can mean simply to form an opinion of someone; "try" makes the court setting plain (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: ustedes / vosotros written out; júzguenlo (L, B); háganle un juicio (R)
decisions.reason: The stressed "you" is written out at every level (meaning decision m1). "Juzgar" keeps its legal sense in Spanish (meaning decision m3); Readable says "hacer un juicio" to make the court setting plain. "La ley de ustedes" avoids the ambiguous "su ley", as at 8:17.

decisions.choice: jugez-le (L, B); faites-lui un procès (R)
alternatives: faites-lui un procès at Balanced too
decisions.reason: French "juger" in a sentence about a law still means to try in court and give a verdict (meaning decision m3), so Balanced can keep it, where the English Balanced needs "try". Readable says it in plain words.

decisions.choice: a lei de vocês
decisions.reason: Pilate means the Law of Moses as the Jewish courts applied it (meaning decision m2), but he speaks of it from outside, as their own law, so it stays lowercase here, as in the English. "A sua lei" could be read as Pilate's own.

decisions.choice: the Jews: the chief priests and their officers who brought Jesus to Pilate
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: They are the ones who led Jesus from Caiaphas (18:28) and who, Pilate says, handed him over (18:35); at 19:6 the chief priests and their officers shout for his death. The word names this group of leaders, not the people: Jesus and his disciples are Jews, and so are many who believed in him (11:45; 12:11).

decisions.choice: not lawful for us: under Roman rule only the governor could order a man's death
alternatives: it was not lawful to execute anyone during the festival
it was not lawful for them to crucify
decisions.reason: When Rome took direct rule of Judea in AD 6, Josephus says the first governor was sent with power over life and death (Jewish War 2.117). Some events seem to go against this: the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7:58), and the execution of James the Lord's brother in AD 62 while there was no governor in the province, for which the high priest was removed from office (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200-203). So the rule may have had exceptions, or such killings may have been unlawful. John's point is plain either way: they need Pilate to sentence Jesus.

decisions.choice: the answer shows that they want a death sentence, not a trial
decisions.reason: Pilate offered them a trial under their own law; their reply shows that they have already decided on death. "For us" is put first for stress: they cannot do it, Pilate can. The purpose clause of verse 32 hangs on this exchange.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: not permitted to execute (B); not allowed to put to death (R)
decisions.reason: "Kill" here means a lawful execution after a sentence, not murder (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: los judíos (L); los dirigentes judíos (B, R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John, as at 1:19: Literal shows the word John wrote; Balanced and Readable name the leaders the context shows (meaning decision m1), so no reader takes it as the whole Jewish people. This applies to 18:36 and 18:38.

decisions.choice: no nos es lícito matar (L); no tenemos autoridad para ejecutar (B); no se nos permite condenar a muerte (R)
decisions.reason: "Kill" here means a lawful execution after a sentence, which Balanced and Readable say (meaning decision m2); the issue is legal authority under Rome.

decisions.choice: les Juifs (L); les chefs juifs (B, R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice for John, first used here in this passage. Literal keeps the word John wrote. Balanced and Readable name the group the context shows, the chief priests and their officers (meaning decision m1): in French, "les Juifs" alone reads as the whole people. In "Mfalme wa Wayahudi" (18:33, 39) and in Pilate's "Myahudi" (18:35) the word means the nation and is kept at every level.

decisions.choice: the word of Jesus: his saying about being lifted up (12:32-33; compare 3:14; 8:28)
alternatives: a saying about being handed over to the Gentiles (Mark 10:33)
decisions.reason: The words "signifying by what kind of death he was about to die" repeat 12:33 exactly, where John explained Jesus's saying "when I am lifted up from the earth". Death by Jewish sentence would have been by stoning (8:59; 10:31); because Jesus is handed to the Roman governor, he will die by the Roman penalty of crucifixion, raised up on a cross.

decisions.choice: so that ... might be fulfilled: what happens carries out what Jesus foretold
decisions.reason: John uses this language for Scripture being fulfilled (12:38; 13:18; 19:24, 36), and here, as at 18:9, for Jesus's own words. The authorities' refusal to try Jesus themselves leads, beyond their intent, to the death he had already named.

decisions.choice: signifying: indicating by a hint, not saying outright
decisions.reason: The verb means to point to something by a sign. Jesus had spoken in a picture ("lifted up"), not in plain words, as at 12:33 and 21:19.

decisions.choice: [This was] (L); This was (B); This happened (R); he would be lifted up on a cross (R)
decisions.reason: The Greek purpose clause hangs on the exchange in verse 31; English needs a main clause, so every level supplies one, Literal in brackets. Readable also says what kind of death was meant, as at 12:33 (meaning decision m1). The narrator, not a character, gives the explanation.

decisions.choice: [Esto fue] (L); Esto fue, Esto pasó (B, R); the words of 12:33; levantado en una cruz (R)
decisions.reason: Spanish needs a main clause for the purpose clause, in brackets at Literal, as at 18:9. Each level repeats its own wording of 12:33, which John repeats exactly (meaning decision m1), and Readable says what kind of death was meant, as there.

decisions.choice: [Cela arriva] (L); C'était (B); Cela est arrivé (R); il serait élevé sur une croix (R)
alternatives: afin que ... without a main clause
decisions.reason: The Greek purpose clause hangs on the exchange in verse 31; French, like English, needs a main clause, Literal in brackets. Readable says what kind of death was meant, with "élevé", the word used for being lifted up in 3:14 and 12:32, and adds "sur une croix" as the English Readable does (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: the words of 12:33 repeated at each level
decisions.reason: John repeats 12:33 exactly (meaning decision m1), so each level uses its Swahili from there: "akionyesha ni kifo cha namna gani atakachokufa", and at Readable "akiinuliwa juu ya msalaba". Literal brackets the supplied main clause, as at 18:9.

am.L: ስለዚህ ጲላጦስ እንደገና ወደ ፕራይቶሪዮን ገባ፤ ኢየሱስንም ጠርቶ፦ «አንተ የአይሁድ ንጉሥ ነህ?» አለው።

decisions.choice: the Jews, in the title: the Jewish nation
decisions.reason: "King of the Jews" is a title for the ruler of the nation, the people as a whole. Rome had given it to Herod the Great (Josephus, Antiquities 14.385), and in the Gospels it is used by Gentiles (Matthew 2:2; John 19:3, 19), while Jews say "King of Israel" (1:49; 12:13). Here the word does not mean the authorities, and the title keeps "the Jews".

decisions.choice: the political charge: claiming to be king without Rome's leave
alternatives: a religious question about the Messiah
decisions.reason: Pilate's first question shows the charge the accusers had brought: that Jesus claimed to be king. Under Rome only a ruler appointed by Rome could hold that title, so the claim was rebellion against Caesar (19:12, 15). Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for rebels, and the charge was written above the cross (19:19).

decisions.choice: you: stressed, perhaps with surprise
decisions.reason: The pronoun is placed first and is not needed in Greek. Pilate may be expressing disbelief that this bound prisoner could claim a throne; the same question opens Jesus's trial before Pilate in all four Gospels (Matthew 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3).

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews, at every level
alternatives: the King of the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: This is a title naming the nation (meaning decision m1), so every level keeps the words John wrote, here and at 18:39, with no footnote. "King" takes a capital as part of a title. "Headquarters" (B) and "palace" (R) follow decision r-en-2 at 18:28.

decisions.choice: el Rey de los judíos, at every level; ¿Tú eres ...? (L), ¿Eres tú ...? (B, R)
decisions.reason: A title naming the nation (meaning decision m1), so every level keeps "los judíos", here and at 18:39; "Rey" takes a capital as part of a title, as at 1:49. Literal puts the stressed "tú" first, as the Greek does (meaning decision m3); at the start of the question it is written plain, elsewhere under the setting.

decisions.choice: le roi des Juifs, at every level, with a lowercase "roi"
decisions.reason: The title names the nation (meaning decision m1), so every level keeps "les Juifs" here and at 18:39 and 19:3. French writes titles of office in lowercase ("le roi", "le gouverneur"), so "roi" has no capital, unlike the English "King".

decisions.choice: Toi, tu es le roi des Juifs ? (L)
decisions.reason: The stressed pronoun, perhaps with surprise (meaning decision m3), is shown in French by a stressed "toi" and the order of a statement spoken as a question. Balanced and Readable ask the plain question. The opening "Toi" is written plainly, as a sentence-initial pronoun.

decisions.choice: Wewe ndiwe Mfalme wa Wayahudi, at every level
decisions.reason: The title names the nation (meaning decision m1), so every level keeps "Wayahudi" and the capital, as at 18:39. "Ndiwe" (you are the one) marks it as a title and carries the stress on "you" (meaning decision m3).

decisions.choice: Pilate to Jesus: "anh" for "you", "tôi" for himself; no deity_pronoun span
decisions.reason: A governor questioning a prisoner speaks down to him but not crudely: "anh". "ngươi" is archaic; "ông" would grant more respect than Pilate shows. Since "anh" is Pilate's word, not the narrator's deity pronoun, it takes no capitalisation span where the English "You" has one. Kept through 18:33-19:11.

decisions.choice: "Vua của người Do Thái" (L); "Vua dân Do Thái" (B, R)
decisions.reason: "dân Do Thái" names the nation, which is the sense in the title; Literal keeps the plain genitive.

decisions.choice: Pilate speaks to Jesus in the plain style (해라체: "네가 ... 이냐?")
decisions.reason: The judge questions a prisoner whom he treats as beneath him; the narrator still uses honorifics for Jesus around the speech. A reviewer may prefer the older 하오체 for the governor. The same through John 18-19.

decisions.choice: "유대인의 왕" at every level
decisions.reason: In the title "the Jews" is the Jewish nation (meaning decision), so Balanced and Readable keep "유대인" here and do not switch to "유대 지도자들".

decisions.choice: Pilate addresses Jesus as "አንተ", the pronoun written out; Jesus answers him with "አንተ"
alternatives: The respectful "እርስዎ" from Jesus to the governor
decisions.reason: As in Matthew 27:11, everyone says "አንተ" to Jesus, and Jesus speaks to one person with "አንተ". The written-out "አንተ" carries the Greek's stressed "you".

vi.B: Đức Giê-xu đáp: "Ông tự hỏi điều này, hay người khác đã nói với ông về {{deity_pronoun:ta|Ta}}?"

ko.L: 예수께서 대답하셨다. "네가 스스로 이 말을 하느냐, 아니면 다른 사람들이 나에 대하여 너에게 말해 주었느냐?"

decisions.choice: from yourself: on your own account, from your own thinking
decisions.reason: The phrase means acting or speaking on one's own initiative, as when Jesus says he does nothing "from himself" (5:19; 7:17) and John says Caiaphas did not speak "from himself" (11:51).

decisions.choice: Jesus asks whose question it is, and so what kind of king is meant
decisions.reason: If the question is Pilate's own, "king" means a rebel against Rome; if it comes from the accusers, it carries their charge, and behind it Israel's hope of an anointed king. Jesus does not deny being a king (18:36-37), but he will not accept the title in the sense of a rival to Caesar. This reading of his purpose is likely from what follows but is not stated.

decisions.choice: asking this on your own (B); your own question (R)
decisions.reason: The idiom "from yourself" is put in plain words (meaning decision m1); Pilate has asked a question, so Balanced and Readable say "asking" and "question". "You" here is Pilate and takes no setting.

decisions.choice: de ti mismo (L); por tu cuenta (B); tu propia pregunta (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the idiom in the form used at 11:51 ("no lo dijo de sí mismo"); Balanced and Readable put it in plain words (meaning decision m1). "Tú" and "ti" here are Pilate and take no setting; "mí" is Jesus and does.

decisions.choice: tu between Jesus and Pilate
decisions.reason: The French brief: one person is addressed with "tu", as in every modern French Bible, whatever his rank; Pilate and Jesus say "tu" to each other, and the accusers say "tu" to Pilate. "Tu" and "te" for Pilate take no setting; those for Jesus do.

decisions.choice: Jesus to Pilate: "ông" for "you", "Ta" for himself
decisions.reason: As the style guide: Jesus calls himself "Ta" and addresses an official as "ông", which is courteous without deference.

decisions.choice: Jesus answers Pilate in the plain style (해라체: "네가 ... 하느냐")
decisions.reason: The style guide gives Jesus 해라체 to everyone except the Father (section 4); a prisoner answering the governor so shows the authority John gives him in the trial. A reviewer may prefer 하오체 here. The same through John 18-19.

decisions.choice: a scornful question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: The question word expects "no", often with impatience, and "I" is stressed. Pilate rejects the idea that he would have any interest of his own in Jewish questions about a king.

decisions.choice: Jew: a member of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: Here the word means the people as a whole, set against Pilate, a Roman and a Gentile. It needs no footnote, since every level keeps it.

decisions.choice: Do you think I am a Jew? (B); Am I a Jew? No! (R)
alternatives: I am not a Jew, am I? (Literal)
decisions.reason: English shows the expected answer and the scorn in different ways (meaning decision m1): Balanced turns it to Jesus with "Do you think", and Readable gives the answer the Greek implies.

decisions.choice: ¿Acaso soy yo judío? (L, R); ¿Crees que yo soy judío? (B); ¡Claro que no! (R); speech running into the next sentence
decisions.reason: "¿Acaso ...?" expects the answer no, as the Greek does, and the stressed "yo" carries the scorn (meaning decision m1); Balanced turns it to Jesus with "¿Crees que ...?", and Readable gives the answer the Greek implies. Pilate's words go on in the next sentence, so the guillemet closes there.

decisions.choice: Suis-je donc juif, moi ? (L); Me prends-tu pour un Juif ? (B); Est-ce que je suis juif ? Bien sûr que non ! (R)
alternatives: Est-ce que je suis juif ? at every level
decisions.reason: The Greek question expects "no", with scorn, and stresses "I" (meaning decision m1). French shows this with "donc" and a stressed "moi" (L), with the idiom "me prends-tu pour" (B), or by giving the answer (R). "Juif" is an adjective after "être" (lowercase) and a noun after "pour un" (capital).

decisions.choice: Kwani ...? (L)
decisions.reason: The Greek question expects "no" and is impatient (meaning decision m1). Swahili "kwani" at the head of a question carries that scorn ("what, am I a Jew?"); a plain "Je" would not. Balanced and Readable follow the English.

decisions.choice: your nation: Israel as a nation, acting through its rulers
alternatives: every member of the Jewish people
decisions.reason: The word is the one the chief priests and Caiaphas use for the nation they rule and claim to protect (11:48-52). In Pilate's mouth it means the nation in its official leadership; the ones he names, and the only ones present in the scene, are the chief priests and those with them (18:28; 19:6). Pilate's words do not say that the Jewish people as a whole handed Jesus over, and John does not say so either.

decisions.choice: your own: the possessive is stressed
decisions.reason: The nation is put first and the possessive is added after it for stress: Jesus's own people, not Rome, brought the case. It answers Jesus's question whether others had told Pilate about him (18:34).

decisions.choice: what did you do: Pilate asks for the actual offense
decisions.reason: Pilate leaves the title aside and asks what Jesus has done, since the accusers named no crime (18:30). Jesus answers about his kingdom instead (18:36).

decisions.choice: your own nation; handed over, at every level
decisions.reason: "Nation" keeps the word Pilate used, the word the leaders used of the people they govern (meaning decision m1), so that no level makes it a statement about the whole people. "Handed over" follows decision r-en-1 at 18:30.

decisions.choice: la nación tuya (L), tu propia nación (B, R); los principales sacerdotes (L), los jefes de los sacerdotes (B, R); entregaron
decisions.reason: "Nación" keeps the word Pilate used, the word the leaders used of the people they govern (11:48-52; meaning decision m1), so no level makes it a statement about the whole people; the possessive is stressed (meaning decision m2). The chief priests as in John 7 and 11; "entregar" as in 18:30.

decisions.choice: ta propre nation
decisions.reason: "Nation" keeps the word the leaders used for the people they govern (11:48-52), which Pilate uses of the nation in its official leadership (meaning decision m1). "Ton peuple" would read as the whole people and make the sentence say more than John does.

decisions.choice: "nộp" for "handed over" at every level
decisions.reason: The same verb runs through the passion story (18:30, 18:35, 18:36, 19:11, 19:16), so Vietnamese keeps one verb for it too.

decisions.choice: not of this world: his kingdom does not have its origin or its authority from this world
alternatives: his kingdom has nothing to do with this world
his kingdom is only spiritual or only future
decisions.reason: "Of" here means coming from, as when Jesus says his disciples are not "of the world" (17:14, 16) though they are in it. His kingship does not rest on the world's power or rise from it; it comes from above (3:31). The closing words "not from here" say the same thing again. "The world" here is humanity in its life apart from God and against him (15:18-19).

decisions.choice: attendants: men who serve under a ruler and act for him, such as guards or officers
decisions.reason: The word is not the one for a slave. It is the word for the officers sent by the chief priests to arrest Jesus (7:32; 18:3, 12) and who struck him (18:22). Jesus says that if his kingdom were the world's kind, he too would have armed men acting for him. Peter's sword was drawn and put away (18:10-11).

decisions.choice: the Jews: the authorities who had Jesus arrested and brought him to Pilate
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of those into whose hands he would have been delivered, the chief priests and their officers who arrested him (18:3, 12) and handed him to Pilate (18:35). He is himself a Jew, and so are the servants he speaks of; the word names the authorities, not the people.

decisions.choice: but now: but as things are, not "at this time"
alternatives: but at present (implying that later it will be from here)
decisions.reason: After an unreal "if", "now" marks the real state of affairs, as in 8:40 and 9:41. It does not hint that the kingdom will become of this world later.

decisions.choice: kingdom: his kingship and rule, not only a territory
decisions.reason: The word means reign and royal power as well as the realm ruled. Jesus answers Pilate's question about whether he is a king (18:33) by speaking of his reign. Apart from 3:3 and 3:5 this is the only place the word occurs in John.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: attendants (L); servants (B); those who serve me (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the narrow sense, men who serve under someone (meaning decision m2). "Servants" is used at Balanced as a natural word for those who act for a king; it is not used here for the word for a slave, which this passage does not have. Readable uses an everyday phrase. "Officers" or "guards" would make Jesus speak of a force he did not have.

decisions.choice: does not come from this world; If it did (B, R); as it is (B)
decisions.reason: "Of this world" can be heard as "has nothing to do with this world"; "come from" gives the sense of origin (meaning decision m1). The repeated phrase is shortened to "If it did". "As it is" gives the sense of "now" (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: es de este mundo (L), viene de este mundo (B, R); el reino mío (L, the Greek order); servidores (L, B), los que me sirven (R); pero ahora (L), Pero, de hecho (B)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "viene de" for the sense of origin (meaning decision m1). The word for those who serve a ruler is not the word for a slave (meaning decision m2), so "siervo" is not used. "Ahora" after an unreal "if" means "as things are" (meaning decision m4), which "de hecho" says at Balanced.

decisions.choice: los dirigentes judíos
decisions.reason: As at 18:31 (meaning decision m3); Literal keeps "los judíos".

decisions.choice: mes serviteurs (L, B); ceux qui me servent (R)
decisions.reason: The word means men who serve under a ruler and act for him (meaning decision m2). "Serviteurs" is free at Literal here, since the word for a slave is rendered "esclave" at that level; "gardes" or "officiers" would give Jesus a force he did not have. Readable uses a verb. "Mais en réalité" (B) gives the sense of "now" after an unreal "if" (meaning decision m4).

decisions.choice: Ufalme {{deity_pronoun:wangu|Wangu}} at the start of the reply
alternatives: Ufalme wangu written plain, as the English "My kingdom"
decisions.reason: The English writes "My" plain because it begins the sentence. In Swahili the possessive follows the noun, so it is not sentence-initial and takes the reader setting like every other "wangu" in the verse.

decisions.choice: wasaidizi (L); watumishi (B); wale wanaonitumikia (R); hautokani na (L), hautoki katika (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek word is the one for officers who act for a ruler, not for slaves (meaning decision m2); Literal says "wasaidizi" (attendants) so that it is not confused with "mtumishi", the Balanced and Readable word for a slave earlier in the chapter. "Kutokana na" and "kutoka katika" give the sense of origin (meaning decision m1), as the English "come from".

decisions.choice: "vương quốc"
decisions.reason: "nước" is the traditional word but today reads first as "country"; "vương quốc" keeps the idea of a king's rule. The meaning decision notes that kingship, not territory, is meant.

decisions.choice: "나라" (L, B); "내가 다스리는 나라" (R)
decisions.reason: "나라" is the usual Korean word for the kingdom (and the one used for "하나님 나라"); Readable adds "다스리는" because "내 나라" alone may be heard as "my country", while the meaning decision speaks of his rule.

decisions.choice: "부하들" (L); "신하들" (B); "나를 섬기는 사람들" (R)
decisions.reason: The word is for men who serve under a ruler and act for him, such as guards (meaning decision); "종" is kept for doulos.

decisions.choice: servidores (L); servos (B)
decisions.reason: Portuguese "servidores" names men in a ruler's service without making them slaves (meaning decision m2); Balanced says "servos", the natural word for those who serve a king, as the English "servants".

decisions.choice: "መንግሥቴ" (my kingdom, my kingship); "አገልጋዮቼ" (my attendants, L, B), "የሚያገለግሉኝ ሰዎች" (those who serve me, R)
decisions.reason: "መንግሥት" means both a kingdom and the reign of a king, as the Greek does. The attendants are men who act for a ruler; "ወታደሮች" would narrow them to soldiers.

decisions.reason: The word marks an inference. Jesus has spoken of "my kingdom" three times (18:36), and Pilate seizes on it. The SBLGNT prints it as a question; it may carry irony.

decisions.choice: a king: without "the"; Pilate no longer says "the King of the Jews"

decisions.choice: after all (B)

decisions.choice: rey, with no article; tú last (L); después de todo (B)
decisions.reason: Pilate now asks whether Jesus is a king of any kind (meaning decision m2), so no level says "el rey". Literal puts the stressed "tú" last, as the Greek does. Balanced shows the inference with "después de todo" (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: You say that I am a king: a yes, but with a reservation about the word
alternatives: a plain yes: "You say rightly that I am a king"
You say it, because I am a king
decisions.reason: The Gospels use the same short answer before the high priest and before Pilate (Matthew 26:64; 27:11; Mark 15:2; Luke 23:3). It does not deny the claim, and Jesus goes on to speak of his kingship; but it leaves the word on Pilate's lips, since Pilate means something Jesus does not. The little word after "say" can also be read as "because", making a firmer yes: "You say so, because I am a king." The evidence does not settle how strong the yes is, so every level keeps the words open.

decisions.choice: You are the one who says (B); It is you who say (R)
decisions.reason: "You" is stressed in Greek. Balanced and Readable show the stress without turning the answer into a plain yes or a plain no (meaning decision m1). "You" here is Pilate and takes no setting.

decisions.choice: Eres tú quien dice (B); Eres tú el que dice (R)
decisions.reason: As in English: the stressed "you" is shown without turning the answer into a plain yes or a plain no (meaning decision m1). "Tú" here is Pilate and takes no setting. The quotation runs on into the next sentence.

decisions.choice: Tu dis que je suis roi (L); C'est toi qui dis que je suis roi (B, R)
alternatives: C'est toi qui le dis : je suis roi
decisions.reason: The traditional French "Tu le dis" is heard today as a plain yes; the Greek answer is a yes with a reservation about the word (meaning decision m1). Keeping "que je suis roi" leaves the word on Pilate's lips, and "c'est toi qui" shows the stressed "you". "Tu" here is Pilate and takes no setting.

decisions.choice: born ... come into the world: his human birth and his coming from God
alternatives: two ways of saying only that he was born
decisions.reason: "I" is stressed. In John, coming into the world is said of one who comes from God (3:19; 6:14; 11:27; 16:28). Jesus speaks of a purpose that goes back before his birth. Pilate hears only the first half.

decisions.choice: testify to the truth: bear witness to God's reality, made known in Jesus
decisions.reason: In John the truth is what God is and what he has made known in his Son (1:14, 17; 8:32; 14:6). Jesus speaks of his kingship in terms of witness, not force: this is how he reigns. Testimony is a thread through the Gospel (1:7; 3:11; 5:31-39).

decisions.choice: of the truth: belonging to the truth, having one's life from it
decisions.reason: "Of" names belonging and origin, as in "whoever is of God hears the words of God" (8:47). Those who belong to the truth recognize Jesus's voice, as his sheep know the voice of the shepherd (10:3-4, 16, 27). Without saying so, Jesus invites Pilate to listen.

decisions.choice: testify (L, B); be a witness to (R); hears my voice (L); listen to my voice (B); listen to me (R)
decisions.reason: "Testify" is used for this verb through John. Hearing here means listening and responding (meaning decision m3), so Balanced says "listen to". Readable drops "voice" for plain speech; the echo of the shepherd's voice (10:3-4) remains at Literal and Balanced.

decisions.choice: dar testimonio (L, B), ser testigo (R); es de la verdad (L), pertenecen a la verdad (B, R); oye (L), escuchan (B, R)
decisions.reason: "Testimonio" is John's witness word throughout (meaning decision m2). "Es de" as at 8:47 Literal, with "pertenecer" at Balanced and Readable for belonging (meaning decision m3). Hearing here is listening and responding, as with the sheep of 10:27, so Balanced and Readable say "escuchar".

decisions.choice: rendre témoignage (L, B); être témoin (R); entend ma voix (L); écoutent ma voix (B); m'écoutent (R)
decisions.reason: "Rendre témoignage" is the book-wide French for this verb; Readable uses the plainer "être témoin", as the English Readable says "be a witness". Literal keeps the plain verb of hearing; Balanced says "écouter", hearing that listens and responds (meaning decision m3), and keeps the voice, the echo of the shepherd (10:3-4). "Quiconque" and "tous ceux qui" are inclusive already and need no gender setting.

decisions.choice: truth: without "the", truth in general
decisions.reason: Jesus spoke of "the truth" he came to testify to (18:37); Pilate asks about truth as an idea. The two are speaking past each other.

decisions.choice: the tone of Pilate's question is not stated
decisions.reason: John does not say how Pilate meant it, and Pilate does not wait for an answer; he goes straight out (18:38b). The reader of the Gospel already knows the answer Jesus has given: "I am the way and the truth and the life" (14:6).

decisions.choice: [la] verdad (L); la verdad (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek has no article (meaning decision m1). Spanish needs one to ask about truth in general; without it the question reads "what is true?". Literal brackets it. No level adds a tone that John does not state (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: la vérité, without brackets
decisions.reason: The Greek has no article: Pilate asks about truth in general (meaning decision m1). French needs the article with an abstract noun used in general ("la vérité", as "la liberté"), so it is part of the grammar and is not bracketed, even at Literal; the difference from "the truth" of verse 37 cannot be shown in French.

decisions.choice: kweli, the same word as in 18:37
decisions.reason: The key term for truth is "kweli" at every level (style guide), so Pilate's question picks up Jesus's word in 18:37 exactly, as in the Greek. Swahili has no article to show that Pilate says "truth" and not "the truth" (meaning decision m1); the meaning note carries it.

decisions.choice: a verdade
decisions.reason: Portuguese uses the article for an abstract noun in general ("O que é a verdade?"), so it cannot copy the missing Greek article; the question still asks about truth as an idea (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: the Jews: the chief priests and their officers waiting outside
alternatives: the Jewish people as a whole
decisions.reason: They are the same group who would not enter the headquarters (18:28) and who brought the charge (18:29-31, 35). John mentions no crowd in the trial; when he names the ones who shout, they are the chief priests and their officers (19:6). Others may have been with them, but the word here names the accusers, not the people.

decisions.choice: case: a legal ground for a charge
decisions.reason: The word means the cause or ground of an accusation. As judge, Pilate finds nothing in Jesus that would support a charge under Roman law. He will say so again twice (19:4, 6).

decisions.choice: I: stressed, the judge's own finding
decisions.reason: Pilate sets his finding as judge against what the accusers claim (18:30).

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities, Balanced and Readable name them (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: no case against him (B); no reason to condemn him (R)
decisions.reason: Pilate speaks as a judge, so Balanced and Readable use the language of a court (meaning decision m2).

decisions.choice: los judíos (L), los dirigentes judíos (B, R); ninguna causa (L), ningún cargo (B), ninguna razón para condenarlo (R)
decisions.reason: The accusers waiting outside (meaning decision m1), named as at 18:31. Pilate speaks as a judge, so each level uses the language of a court (meaning decision m2); "causa" is the legal word for a case.

decisions.choice: aucun grief (L); aucun motif d'accusation (B); aucune raison de le condamner (R)
decisions.reason: The word is the legal ground for a charge (meaning decision m2). "Grief" is the French legal word for a ground of complaint; "motif d'accusation" is plainer, and Readable says what the finding means. "Faute" or "crime" would make it a moral verdict. The same words are used in 19:4 and 19:6.

decisions.choice: "아무 죄목도 찾지 못한다" (L); "아무 죄도 찾지 못하겠다" (B); "처벌할 이유를 하나도 찾지 못하겠다" (R); the same at 19:4 and 19:6
decisions.reason: The word is a legal ground for a charge; Literal keeps the judge's term, Balanced uses the common "죄", and Readable says what it means for the prisoner. Kept the same in all three findings so the repetition is heard.

decisions.choice: "የክስ ምክንያት" (ground for a charge, L), "የሚያስከስስ ነገር" (anything to charge him with, B), "የሚያስፈርድበት ምክንያት" (a reason to condemn him, R); the same at 19:4 and 19:6
decisions.reason: The Greek word is a legal ground for a charge; "ጥፋት" would make Pilate pronounce on Jesus's character rather than on the case.

decisions.choice: a custom of releasing one prisoner at Passover
decisions.reason: All four Gospels speak of this custom (Matthew 27:15; Mark 15:6; Luke 23:18). No other ancient source mentions such a release in Judea, though rulers elsewhere did sometimes free prisoners at festivals. Pilate calls it "your" custom: a favor to the people at their feast of freedom from slavery in Egypt.

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews: the title of the charge, the Jewish nation
decisions.reason: As at 18:33, the title names the nation. In Pilate's mouth it may be mocking, aimed at the accusers as much as at Jesus (19:14-15).

decisions.choice: one: one prisoner
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "one"; the context shows that a prisoner is meant. "You" throughout is plural, the people outside.

decisions.choice: one [man] (L); one prisoner, set free (B, R)
decisions.reason: English needs a noun for "one" (meaning decision m3). "King of the Jews" is kept at every level, as at 18:33 (decision r-en-1 there).

decisions.choice: a uno (L); a un preso (B, R); el Rey de los judíos
decisions.reason: Spanish "a uno" can stand alone, so Literal needs no bracket; Balanced and Readable say "preso" (meaning decision m3). Every "you" is plural, the people outside, and takes the setting. "Rey de los judíos" as at 18:33.

decisions.choice: un [prisonnier] (L); un prisonnier (B, R); relâcher (L); libérer (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says only "one"; French needs a noun, and "prisonnier" is what the context shows (meaning decision m3), bracketed at Literal. "Relâcher" is the legal word for releasing a prisoner; Balanced and Readable use the commoner "libérer".

decisions.choice: again: though John has told of no earlier shouting
alternatives: an earlier outcry the reader is meant to assume
decisions.reason: John has not mentioned any shouting before this. "Again" may assume that the accusers had already been loud in their demands, or may mean simply "in turn". It does not change what they said.

decisions.choice: shouted: cried out loudly
decisions.reason: The same verb describes the crowd's "Hosanna" at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem (12:13) and the shouts of "Crucify!" (19:6, 15).

decisions.choice: Barabbas: an Aramaic name meaning "son of the father"
decisions.reason: John does not explain the name, and he does not say who Barabbas was until the next sentence. The name was an ordinary one; any wordplay with Jesus as the Son of the Father is not drawn out by John.

decisions.choice: Not this one! Barabbas! (B); Not this man! Give us Barabbas! (R)
decisions.reason: A shout is short, so Balanced breaks it in two. Readable supplies "Give us" to make plain what they want.

decisions.choice: ¡A ese no! ¡A Barrabás! (B); ¡Queremos a Barrabás! (R)
decisions.reason: As in English: a shout is short, so Balanced breaks it in two, and Readable says plainly what they want.

decisions.choice: the crowd's shouted demands to Pilate in 하오체 ("바라바요", "풀어 주시오"); their spoken arguments in 합쇼체
alternatives: 합쇼체 ("풀어 주십시오") for the shouts too
decisions.reason: A shouting crowd in 합쇼체 sounds too polite, and 해라체 would make them address the governor as an inferior; 하오체 keeps a blunt, public respect. The same for the shouts in 19:6 and 19:15; the argument of 19:12 stays in 합쇼체.

records.literal_gloss: Was now the Barabbas a bandit.

vi.L: Còn Ba-ra-ba là một kẻ cướp.

decisions.choice: bandit: a violent robber, possibly a rebel against Rome
decisions.reason: The word is the one used in 10:1 and 10:8 for the bandit who climbs into the sheepfold. It means a robber who uses violence, and in the first century it was also used of armed men who rose against Roman rule. Mark 15:7 and Luke 23:19 say that Barabbas was in prison for an uprising and for murder, so he may have been such a rebel.

decisions.choice: the closing remark: the people's choice set beside the shepherd and the king
decisions.reason: John ends the scene with four words. The man chosen is the kind Jesus named in 10:1, 8 as the opposite of the good shepherd, and a man of violence is preferred to a king whose servants do not fight (18:36). The irony is left unspoken.

decisions.choice: bandit, at every level
decisions.reason: The same English word as in 10:1 and 10:8, so that readers can hear the echo (meaning decision m2). The footnote gives "rebel" (meaning decision m1).

decisions.choice: bandido, at every level
decisions.reason: The same word as in 10:1 and 10:8, so that readers can hear the echo (meaning decision m2); the footnote of meaning decision m1 gives "rebel".

decisions.choice: un bandit, at every level
decisions.reason: "Bandit" is the everyday French word for a violent robber, and the same word should be used in 10:1 and 10:8 so that readers hear the echo (meaning decision m2). "Brigand" is older; "rebelle" is a possible sense given in the footnote of meaning decision m1.

decisions.choice: mnyang'anyi at every level
decisions.reason: The same word as for the bandit in 10:1 and 10:8, so the echo noted in meaning decision m2 is kept. "Mnyang'anyi" is a robber who takes by force; the footnote's "rebel" belongs to the meaning notes.

decisions.choice: "ወንበዴ" (bandit) at every level
decisions.reason: "ወንበዴ" is a violent robber who lives outside the law, the word Matthew 26:55 uses for the same Greek word; "ሌባ" is too mild, and "ዓመፀኛ" would decide a question the meaning decision leaves open.
